#7721. 20 Ways to Keep Warm Without Turning on the Heat

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:38 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When winter winds blow, some homeowners dread the accompanying—and often outrageous— heating bills that Jack Frost brings with him. Heating oil prices for 2026, which are topping $6 a gallon, are particularly painful; overall, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), homeowners can expect to pay an average of 8.7 percent more to heat their homes than they did last winter.

While you probably won’t get away with not turning on the heat at all this winter, these smart solutions can help minimize winter’s impact on your budget.

Drafty windows are some of the biggest culprits when it comes to heat loss, which is why it’s important to insulate them properly. For an inexpensive fix, cut a piece of bubble wrap to fit perfectly inside the window frame, spray a thin film of water on the window, and press the bubble wrap into the glass. The layer of plastic will let the sunlight in while keeping the warmth where it belongs: inside.

The 3M window insulation kit is 0.75 mils thick and comes in one cut-to-fit sheet that measures 17.5 feet long by 5.16 feet wide.   Read the review.

Warm air rises, which isn’t great news for our heating bills. Although it might seem as though switching your ceiling fan on would make your room colder rather than warmer, turning on the fan can actually make a room toastier so long as you set the blades to spin in a clockwise manner.

To reverse the direction of your ceiling fan, check for a switch at the base of your fan. This change of direction creates a slight updraft that will push the warm air toward the walls and back down into the room.

Air leaks are a major source of heat loss. Check your home for possible gaps with this easy test: Hold a piece of toilet paper in front of your window and door frames. If the toilet paper moves, you’ve found a crack that needs to be sealed. Use weatherstripping to fill the gaps so that the heat stays tucked inside, and consider adding foam insulation to outlets to reduce heat loss even more. Caulk, too, is a useful weapon against leaks. “Use caulk for stationary cracks and gaps, especially around window frames or where siding meets the home’s foundation,” says HVAC technician Josh Mitchell, who works with AirConditionerLab in Nevada City, Calif.

RELATED: The 20 Best Products for Surviving Winter

If you have radiators in your home, try fashioning reflective plates out of aluminum foil and placing one behind each unit. Instead of just heating up your wall, the radiator will heat the foil, which will reflect warmth back into the room and allow you to maximize the unit’s output.

Exhaust fans are effective at ridding your bathroom of humid air during and after a hot shower. But leaving the fan off altogether when you shower is a good strategy for room heat generation, one that works particularly well if you leave the bathroom door open while you shower. The steam warms the air in the bathroom, and in adjacent halls and rooms.

If you have drafty doors, craft an inexpensive DIY fix from foam pipe insulation. Cut the foam to size, and wrap it around the bottom of your doors—yes, even the interior ones!—to prevent heat from escaping and utility costs from going up. If you’re not up for a project, there are plenty of affordable draft dodgers you can purchase. Draft dodgers are easy to slide off the door when the weather warms up, so you have no excuse not to try this budget-saving solution.

If you don’t have a jacket for your water heater, odds are you’re letting its warmth go to waste. Consider insulating your unit to reduce heat loss and save a little cash—about $20 a month, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. To see if your water heater needs additional insulation, just touch it. If it feels warm, it could probably use a water heater blanket, but check your owner’s manual first to make sure it’s safe to cover your model.

RELATED: Solved! When to Replace a Water Heater, Explained

This is by far the easiest thing you can do to lower home heating bills: Raise the blinds and open the curtains when the sun is out. It’s especially important to keep window coverings open on south-facing windows, because they bring in the warmest afternoon sun. Just remember to close your curtains again at night to keep all the toasty air inside until the sun returns.

Consider replacing your thermostat with a smart thermostat, which “allows you to set different temperature schedules throughout the day based on your occupancy patterns,” according to Justin Bohannon of Affordable Solutions HVAC & Electrical in Durham, North Carolina. “By utilizing setback temperatures during times of lower demand, such as when you’re at work or sleeping, you can save energy and reduce heating costs,” he adds.

Iced coffee or iced tea may be your go-to beverage to help you get through the day, but come winter it might be time to make the switch to a warmer beverage. Hot cocoa, tea, and coffee will warm you up on the inside and still give you that kick of caffeine you need.

A top sheet and comforter might be plenty comfortable from spring to fall, but in winter, it’s time to burrow under multiple layers. Try making your bed with flannel sheets and fleece or electric blankets, then drop your thermostat down a couple of degrees at nighttime to stay warm without burning through extra cash.

Cozying up next to a roaring fire is a way to warm up that comes with a caveat. In traditional fireplaces, about 80 percent of the heat generated escapes up the chimney. In fact, an open fireplace can even suck warm air out of the room. So while you do get some warmth from a fire in the fireplace, it may be less than you might think. To maximize your fireplace’s heat output, consider upgrading it with energy-efficient, wood-burning inserts.

If you do light a fire in the fireplace, remember to close the flue after you have put the fire out (keep the flue open, of course, while the fire is burning). Otherwise, all the warm air will go up and out of the house and let in the frigid air from outside.

RELATED: 11 Mistakes You Should Never Make With Your Fireplace

Layering clothing can goes a long way toward keeping you warm. While you’re at home, wear long sleeves, and wear socks (maybe even heated socks) and slippers around the house. Fashion retailer Uniqlo sells shirts, undershirts, long underwear, leggings, and socks with Heattech technology that traps heat to keep you warm. When you can’t shake a chill, throw your sweatshirt in the dryer for a quick spin to warm it up.

Check all your air vents to make sure they aren’t covered by window treatments or furniture. “Rearranging furniture is a surprisingly effective way to reduce home heating bills,” says Guy Sharp, a relocation manager at Andorra Guides who help residents settle into new homes, with a special focus on staying warm on a budget in the chilly temperatures that characterize the small European country nestled in the Pyrenees mountains.

“When you position your furniture away from radiators, baseboard heaters, and vents, you allow the heat to circulate freely throughout the room,” he adds. Blocked vents also makes your furnace work harder than it should and increases air pressure in the ductwork, which can lead to cracks. If it’s not possible to rearrange your furniture, you can use vent extenders to direct air around obstructions.

If you have an attic, it’s a good idea to confirm that there’s sufficient insulation up there and that the insulation is properly affixed. Look for gaps around pipes and ducts, and make sure that there aren’t any loose bits. Add more attic insulation if you find that what’s there could use some shoring up.

If your floors feel cold, throwing down some area rugs can will warm your feet up in a jif. Rugs offer a barrier against chilly air rising up from your concrete foundation, or from the crawl space under your home. For even more insulation (and to keep the rugs from slipping), use rug pads under your rugs.

If your home has seldom-used rooms, close them off. There’s no sense in heating the guest room, for example, if you’re not expecting visitors for a while. “Also make sure that you close any vents in little-used rooms,” says Leonard Ang, CEO of iPropertyManagement, an online company that offers advice for landlords, investors, and tenants throughout the United States.

For a thorough evaluation of how to best protect your home against winter’s chill, consider scheduling an energy assessment or energy audit. In such an audit, professionals use special equipment that draws in air through any gaps in your home’s exterior, allowing them to pinpoint areas that should be sealed or insulated.

When you do eventually turn on the heat, make sure your furnace is ready for a season of use. Having your furnace serviced in the fall is an often overlooked step that can help you save money on winter heating costs. “Regular maintenance of your heating system ensures it operates at peak efficiency,” says Brad Roberson, president of Aire Serv, an HVAC service company that has locations around the country.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

#7718. City's Using Meta Moderation Assist Feature for Facebook Comments Doesn't Violate First Amendment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Ruth Bermudez Montenegro (S.D. Cal.) Oct. 22 in Jalisi v. City of Poway:

The City of Poway … maintains a public Facebook page where it "posts updates about various items that may be of interest to [City] residents and the general public." The Facebook page is open to public comment, and members of the public routinely comment on posts on the page. Plaintiff is a resident of Poway who has criticized aspects of the City's decisions for several years, including by speaking during city council meetings, corresponding with City officials, and posting critical comments on the City's Facebook page. City officials and staff, including those responsible for the Facebook page, appear to recognize Plaintiff as a critic.

Several times during the past year, Plaintiff's comments on the City's Facebook page have been "hidden" or "shadow banned;" that is, his comments are not deleted and are still visible when Plaintiff looks at the posts, but are not visible when other Facebook users look at the posts. The City's Social Media Policy provides that "[t]he City's social media presence serves as a limited public forum and all content shall be monitored and moderated." The Policy indicates that user-generated posts will be deleted if those posts, among other things: "use[ ] abusive, vulgar, offensive, profane, sexual, threatening, deliberately untruthful or defamatory language or content." Additionally, "[p]ostings from a public user account which contain inappropriate or disruptive content, … or believed to be spam, may result in the public user account being blocked from any further activity on the City's social media account … at the discretion of the City Manager's Office."

Plaintiff believes that the City is hiding his comments because it wants to suppress his critical viewpoints…. The City represents that none of its employees have ever hidden or removed any comments made by Plaintiff; instead, Meta's Moderation Assist Program has hidden these comments because it has flagged Plaintiff's Facebook profile as a "non-human 'bot'" account. Meta Moderation Assist "is necessary because the City does not have the resources nor ability to actively monitor each and every comment made in real time in order to manually hide bot comments, particularly considering these comments can be submitted 24 hours a day seven days a week." The City believes that Plaintiff's comments were hidden because Moderation Assist flagged him as a bot: "Moderation Assist will automatically hide a post if (1) the commenter does not have any friends or followers, (2) the comment has a link, or (3) the commenter does not have a profile picture." Plaintiff does not have a profile picture, has only one Facebook friend, and has no posts on his own profile, which "are typically strong indicators that the account is a non-human bot."

The city agreed that viewpoint-based moderation of Jalisi's posts would be unconstitutional, and agreed to "… manually unhiding Plaintiff's prior Facebook posts." But it opposed Plaintiff's request to "remove any restriction that causes Plaintiff's comments on the City Page to be hidden from the public"; it argued that it needed to keep using the Moderation Assist program, and couldn't turn it off only for Jalisi. And the court held in favor of the city as to this:

[T]he Court need decide whether the City's Facebook page is a limited public forum or a designated public forum. Even when considering laws regulating expression in "quintessential public forums," courts "ask first whether the law is content based or content neutral." …

As a threshold matter, based on the limited and preliminary record before it, the Court notes it is likely that Plaintiff's comments were hidden not by a City policy, but by the Meta Moderation Assist Program. But even assuming … that the restrictive effects of the Meta Moderation Assist Program may be attributed to the City, the Court does not find the restrictions unconstitutional.

First, the restriction is facially content neutral. Based on the Carmichael Declaration, profiles are not flagged as bots by "examin[ing] the content of the message that is conveyed." Rather, they are flagged based on the presence of certain predictive factors, such as the absence of a profile picture or the absence of other Facebook friends. Thus, determining whether a comment may be hidden has nothing to do with the content of the comment.

Second, the restriction can be "justified without reference to the content of the regulated speech" and there is no sign that the restriction was "adopted by the government because of disagreement with the message [the speech] conveys." The City uses Meta Moderation Assist because it "does not have the resources nor ability to actively monitor each and every comment made in real time in order to manually hide bot comments." There is nothing in the record to suggest that the City turned to Meta Moderation Assist "motivated by disagreement with any particular expressive" conduct. Indeed, Plaintiff's evidence that identical comments published by other users remained visible actually strengthens the finding that the restriction is content neutral; critical speech is clearly tolerated by the City. Therefore, the Court finds that the restriction is content neutral and applies intermediate scrutiny.

To survive intermediate scrutiny, the restriction must "'further[ ] an important or substantial governmental interest,' that interest must be 'unrelated to the suppression of free expression,' and the 'incidental restriction on alleged First Amendment freedoms [must be] no greater than is essential to the furtherance of that interest.'"

The City asserts that its interest in using Meta Moderation Assist is "prevent[ing] non-human 'bot' spam postings on its Facebook page, which can overwhelm public pages and make it much more difficult for the public to both obtain important information and participate in the conversation." The Court finds that the two-way exchange of information between the citizenry and the City is a substantial governmental interest.

Furthermore, that interest is "unrelated to the suppression of free expression." In fact, the interest runs counter to the suppression of free expression; it seeks to ensure that residents have effective access to the exchange of ideas with their neighbors and their government. The interest is related to the suppression of expression by non-human bots, but bots are neither "human beings with First Amendment rights" nor the "[corporations] … composed of [them … that] possess First Amendment rights themselves."

Finally, although the record shows there are "incidental restriction[s]" on speech, such as the hiding of comments posted by human beings flagged as bots, those "incidental restriction[s]" are "no greater than essential to the furtherance" of the governmental interest here. "A critical feature of this inquiry turns on whether the [government] seriously undertook to address the problems it faces with less intrusive tools readily available to it." Again, on the early record before it, the Court finds that the City has no alternative methods to prevent non-human bot accounts from flooding their Facebook page. This is not a situation where there is an obvious, alternative method of regulation that would achieve the governmental interest and incidentally censor no speech….

Alan B. Fenstermacher and Jayson A. Parsons (Rutan & Tucker) represent the City.

NEXT: "Would 'Go Luigi'" Was a Threat, and Thus Subject to Harassment Prevention Order Statute

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7716. Get a Head Start on Your Spring Garden by Planting These Perennials Now

By Nina Malkin, Gretchen Heber, Updated by Teresa Odle

Published Nov 4, 2026 4:04 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Perennials can live for years or even decades, beautifying your garden with very little care. Flowering perennials typically produce blooms by the second year, though some will burst with color the very first year. Spring-blooming perennials signal the coming of warmer weather and more colorful gardens.

However, fall, with its combination of still-warm soil and cooler, wetter weather, presents an ideal opportunity to encourage root growth in new spring perennials. So admire this list of perennials to plant in fall, pick your favorites, and take advantage of planting spring-blooming perennial flowers before winter strikes.

Planting perennials in the still-warm fall soil gives the plants a chance to get established underground, building a strong root system that will prepare them for vigorous aboveground growth—and flowering—come springtime. This helps lessen the risk of heat and water stress in spring. In addition, fall planting is beneficial in drought-prone areas. According to High Country Gardens, “as plants begin to go dormant in fall, and their energy shifts from top growth to root growth, they use much less water.”

With cooler fall soil and typically less windy conditions than spring, weather tends to stress young plants less in autumn. If you live where it’s still blisteringly hot, wait until temperatures cool down, but don’t wait so long that the plants have little to no chance to get somewhat established before a freeze hits.

Many perennial plants fare better with a fall planting and are better able to produce flowers in spring. Several of the plants on this list are herbaceous perennials, which typically die back to the ground in winter anyway, but remain alive underground and leaf out in spring, so they are well suited for fall planting. As with any new plant, don’t expect your fall-planted perennial to reach its mature size and full flowering in its first year, but give it some time to establish.

If you get impatient for posies as the winter drags on, put in hellebores now. Summer is too hot for them, so these are among the best perennials to plant in fall. Also known as Lenten rose, this is one of the first flowers to appear each year, often poking through the snow in late winter or early spring with big, bowl-shaped pink, yellow, or maroon blooms. Hardy hellebores do best in slightly shaded spots and neutral to alkaline soils with good drainage. Though deer and rabbits avoid munching on hellebores, the plants’ leaves, stems, and sap are poisonous if ingested.

Best For: Early blooming in a mass planting or ground cover.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 8Size: 12 to 15 inches tallLight: Dappled sunlight to partial shade

Certainly no shrinking violet, pasque flower is a showstopper with purple bell-shaped blossoms that is native to dry meadows in parts of Europe. Pasque is the Old French word for “Easter,” and this perennial is bound to bloom in time for the holiday (fortunately, it is also rabbit-resistant). The gorgeous garden star, which is also known as windflower and meadow anemone, flourishes in fertile soil with good drainage for easy purple spring flowers. Plant it in August if possible to give it time to produce blooms.

Best For: Winter to early spring color in cooler zones.USDA hardiness zones: 4 to 8Size: 4 to 10 inches tallLight: Partial shade to full sun

For colorful ground cover, consider creeping phlox. Phlox is the Greek word for “fire,” and this mat-forming plant will set your landscape ablaze with small, flat, fragrant blooms in purple, pink, red, or white beginning in March. It’s a favorite for filling in rock gardens and can be especially pretty draping over a wall. Choose a spot that receives dappled sun and has sandy soil that drains well. Though phlox might need dividing if it gets too crowded, it is a low-maintenance ground cover.

Best For: Colorful spring-blooming groundcover or to drape over walls or rocks.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 6 inches tallLight: Dappled shade to full sun

Gardeners who don’t like a lot of toil may love growing Virginia bluebells. Plant them in fall and In early spring, the perennial pops out flowers that start pale and turn a rich, true blue. They thrive in moist soil and mostly shady conditions, eventually establishing a colony of pollinator-friendly ground cover filled with foolproof flowers that require virtually zero care.

Best For: True blue color in moist woodland gardens. USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 1.5 to 2 feet tallLight: Partial to full shade

Prized for its graceful, nodding blooms, columbine is a woodland perennial, so it likes a partly shaded location and consistently moist soil. Its white, yellow, red, or blue flowers appear in early spring and bloom through midsummer. These native flowers also are deer- and rabbit-resistant, a plus in gardens visited by wildlife. The only caveat is that columbine is one of the shorter-lived perennials; if you love them, add a few plants every year or so to keep their color going and the butterflies and hummingbirds happy in mountain, forested, and cooler growing zones.

Best For: Spring color in natural and woodland gardens or meadows.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 1 to 3 feet tallLight: Partial shade to full sun

Tall, resilient false indigo (also known as blue wild indigo) flowers in late spring through fall with thick stalks and spires of small dark-blue blooms. If blue isn’t your bag, check out hybrids in other colors, including yellow and pink. False indigo likes full sun but can deal with some shade and is best planted in fall in hotter climates. The drought-tolerant native that’s a member of the pea family beckons bees and butterflies, and is unlikely to get nibbled by deer and rabbits.

Best For: Blue flowers above oval blue-green leaves in drought-tolerant gardens USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 3 to 4 feet high and wideLight: Partial shade to full sun

It must be those long, fuzzy, pale-colored flowers that give Astilbe its common nickname: false goat’s beard. This practically trouble-free plant that blooms from spring through summer is especially popular as a shady border plant and for its deer resistance. Its flowers contrast well against broad, leafy foliage. Astilbe thrives in loamy, slightly acidic soil and usually needs dividing every 3 to 4 years.

Best For: Border plant for part shade in gardens with acidic soil.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 1 to 4 feet tallLight: Shade to part shade

Attention gardeners in the Southwest who can’t get by on cactus alone: Hartweg’s or Texas sundrops are a perfect perennial pick, flowering in March through October. Also called evening primrose, this night-blooming perennial features flowers with bright yellow petals that open around sunset and remain through the next day. Once classified as Oenothera, the low-growing plant thrives in regions with hot prairies and plains. Sow seeds or plant in partly shaded areas for earlier opening times.

Best For: Large yellow flowers that bloom in the evening for rock gardens or moon gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 9Size: 1 to 1.5 feet high and 2 feet wideLight: Part afternoon shade to full sun

Shade happens—and that’s not a problem for lamium. This lovely yet tough ground cover can easily take on bare spots like those beneath trees. Lamium boasts variegated foliage in silver, gold, and green along with dainty pink and purple flowers that appear in late spring and summer. This rugged plant can thrive in clay and alkaline soils, and it actually prefers dry conditions. Deadhead the flowers once they fade to encourage a new crop of blooms.

Best For: Ground cover under trees or other areas where sun transitions to shade.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: Less than 12 inches high with 2- to 3-foot spreadLight: Partial to full shade

For a flowering perennial that smells as nice as it looks, let dianthus adorn your landscape. Some dianthus species are biennial (living about 2 years) and they require fall planting so they can gain energy over winter. All types offer clusters of spunky spring-through-summer blooms in a range of hues, including pink, white, yellow, and red against blue-green leaves. Dianthus loves sun and well-draining soil, and is ideal for rock gardens, containers, and borders. Its rich nectar will attract pollinators, yet deer and bunnies won’t bother with it.

Best For: Sun-loving flower for rock gardens, containers, and along rock walls. USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 6 to 12 inches high; 6 to 24 inches wideLight: Full sun

This cold-hardy daisy can add a touch of elegance to borders and garden beds. In late spring and early summer, the daisy comes alive with large white flowers with yellow centers, adding a contrast to other perennial garden flowers. The flowers fare best in rich soil with good drainage and are among perennial flowers to plant in fall (or sow from seeds). Shasta daisy is a flower that can handle heat. And while it does well with regular watering, it handles short periods of drought better than soggy soil. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the blooms coming, and even cut fresh ones for flower arrangements.

Best For: Sunny butterfly or cutting gardens or in containers. USDA hardiness zones: 4 to 9Size: 1 to 4 feet high; 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun

Add a pincushion plant to your garden and enjoy the springtime reward of delicate lavender, pink, or white flowers borne on gangly stalks that rise from a clump of gray-green leaves. Perennial in all but the coldest regions, pincushion flower is moderately drought-tolerant, attracts butterflies and hummingbirds, and thrives in sunny spots of the garden. The cut flowers of this plant make a wonderful, somewhat quirky, addition to a bouquet. Sow the seeds in fall.

Best For: Rock gardens or sunny fairy gardens and along walkways.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 9Size: About 1 foot high and wideLight: Full sun

A springtime profusion of plum-colored blooms greets those who plant purple coneflower or sow its seeds thickly in fall. The large, daisy-like flowers sit high above the medium-green foliage on this clumping plant. This hardy perennial can take a bit of shade but needs some sun to produce its stunning blooms. Purple coneflower is not terribly picky about soil, but will do best in soil that drains well. It’s also fairly drought-tolerant once established, and wilts a bit when it needs water. Harvest the blooms to add to indoor flower arrangements.

Best For: Native and butterfly gardens or meadows, or behind lower-growing flowers.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 3 to 4 feet high; 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun but can handle partial shade

Occasionally referred to as tickseed, and recently reclassified as Anacis, this pretty flowering plant is most commonly known as coreopsis. It comes in both annual and perennial varieties. If you’re planting in the fall, be sure to look for a perennial variety. The profuse bloomer produces scads of yellow flowers throughout spring and summer, and even into autumn. Deadhead spent flowers to encourage this long bloom time. Coreopsis is drought-tolerant and deer-resistant, but it will attract pollinators and songbirds.

Best For: Natural areas in rocky or sandy soil, rock gardens, and butterfly gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 3 to 4 feet tall; 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun or light shade

The delicate, intricate flowers of Oenothera lindheimeri (also known as gaura or whirling butterflies), are said to resemble supercharged butterflies. With white-tipped pink “wings” that surround long white stamens topped with yet more pink, gaura provides an elegant feature in the garden. This loose, shrubby plant is native to Texas, Louisiana, and Mexico, and it’s drought- and heat-resistant.

Best For: Native or prairie-style gardens or areas with sandy, well-draining soil.USDA hardiness zones: 5 to 9Size: Flower stems to 4 or 5 feet; about 2 feet wideLight: Full sun

This member of the mint family offers both attractive purple flowers for bees in late spring and aromatic foliage is considered an herb that can go into teas or savory dishes. It’s a reliable plant that can stand alone in a rock garden or spread to form a border along a path. Catmint needs no fertilizer and will rebloom if you shear the plants to remove the first bloom of flowers. Plant it in fall in time to establish some roots before frost. It prefers good drainage and can thrive in rocky or sandy soil. It’s also drought-tolerant and deer-resistant.

Best For: Borders and walkways or in pollinator rock gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 8Size: 1 to 3 feet high, 1 to 2 feet wideLight: Full sun

Add bleeding heart to your garden in fall, and come springtime it will bring arching stems bearing delicate 1- to 2-inch-long heart-shaped pink flowers. An herbaceous, bushy plant formerly known as Dicentra, bleeding heart has clumps of foliage that can go dormant in heat while flower stalks rise above it. Plant this one in part shade, in moist, well-draining soil with plenty of organic material. As summer wears on, bleeding heart will likely retreat, but it will be back on display after winter subsides.

Best For: Woodland gardens, interplanted with foliage ground covers.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 2 to 3 feet high and about 2 feet wideLight: Partial to full shade

A sprawling, almost vine-like shrub, lantana decorates hot landscapes in late spring and summer with masses of delicate flower clusters in purple, orange, pink, yellow, red, or white. It is drought-tolerant once established and although it loves heat, it can feature in summer annual flower beds or containers in slightly cooler climates. Depending on where it grows, lantana can become shrub size. Butterflies flock to this hardy plant, which is deer-, pest-, and disease-resistant. Bear in mind that lantana is toxic to livestock, cats, and dogs.

Best For: Hot areas and drought-tolerant gardens to attract butterflies and hummingbirds.USDA hardiness zones: 7 to 11Size: 1 to 6 feet high; 3 to 5 feet wide where perennialLight: Full sun

Yarrow blooms from spring to fall with masses of umbrella-shaped flower heads gracing the tops of tall stems bearing fern-like foliage. Popular as a cut flower, yarrow is also beautiful in the landscape. You’ll find yarrow in a rainbow of colors, including yellow, pink, red, white, and gold. It’s drought- and heat-tolerant, but yarrow seeds need a cool period to germinate, so it’s best to sow seeds in the fall. Yarrow can spread aggressively, so plant it in a place where you’d like to see a sea of color.

Best For: Naturalized areas like meadows and drought-tolerant butterfly gardens.USDA hardiness zones: 3 to 9Size: 1 to 3 feet high and wideLight: Full sun

Many spurge types offer early spring color, and cushion spurge is no exception. Its small yellow flowers are surrounded by yellow/pale green bracts, creating the impression of a larger flower. The mounded plant can grow in poor soil like sand or in loamy soil. Although the plant thrives in sun, it might need a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates. It’s drought-, deer-, and pest-resistant, and easy to grow and maintain. However, its milky sap is slightly toxic and can cause itching on contact.

Best For: Small spaces in rock or cottage gardens, containers.USDA hardiness zones: 4 to 8Size: 1½ feet high and wideLight: Full sun with some partial shade

Create the feeling of your own “poppy field” or Georgia O’Keefe painting with oriental poppies. Though the flower petals are paperlike, they are large and full of interest around the center. Look for varieties in classic deep red, orange, coral, or even white. Sow seeds or plant nursery transplants about a month before your first expected frost to aim for blooms in late spring to early summer. Note that these flowers do best in cooler and drier regions of the country and require soil that drains well.

Best For: Asian or cottage garden mixed in with late summer bloomersUSDA hardiness zones: 3 to 7Size: 3 feet high and nearly 2 feet wideLight: Dappled to full sunlight

Gardeners in warm regions might want to consider planting Mexican bush sage or other salvias in fall to establish good root systems before spring. In its northern ranges, this big beauty might go all the way to the ground in winter, but it will come roaring back in spring. Mexican bush sage forms an ever-expanding clump of stalks bearing long leaves and velvety purple flower spikes. It thrives in sunny, hot locations and is drought-tolerant once established.

Best For: Borders, mass plantings, or butterfly gardens, especially on slopes.USDA hardiness zones: 7 to 10Size: 3 feet high and 3 feet wideLight: Partial shade to full sun

Spring is typically the time that plants are plentiful from nurseries, and that’s usually when many gardeners are ready to improve their landscapes. But there are garden centers and online sellers that have stock through fall (and even end-of-season sales) or seeds for fall sowing. Keep these tips in mind for fall planting:

The earlier you can plant spring-blooming perennials in fall, the better. This typically is 6 weeks before the average first frost, so you can often plant perennials in September. This gives plants warm soil with cool nights and time to set roots, which can help prevent frost heave. This happens when thawing of frozen ground pushes plants up out of the soil. If some roots have taken hold and you have mulched the ground, the plant has a better shot. However, avoid planting on hot days or less than a month before frost is expected.

Although rule is a strong word for this principle and doesn’t apply to all flowering perennials, knowing about the “3 years” can help gardeners care for their new plants with realistic expectations about how they will look.  • The first year, most perennials need to grow roots, so they might not show much growth above the ground or flower as advertised; give them extra water to help the roots establish.  • In their second season, plants begin to grow a little more but modestly and might display more flowers.  • By the third year, perennials begin to shine and flower as expected; they also might need pruning.

Yes, fall is a good time to plant many, but not all, perennials. One reason is that you have lived with your landscape for a summer and might be ready to add some color for the next year. Most of all, the combination of still-warm soil but cooler nights helps transplants ease into their new home without the stress of heat or cooler spring soil so the roots have a chance to establish for better spring health. Just be aware of your average first frost date and be sure to count backward when adding spring-flowering plants in fall.

It’s best to wait and plant bare-root plants in late winter to early spring while they still are dormant, not in fall. This can include roses and other shrubs or fruiting trees. Perennial bulbs to plant in fall will bloom in spring, but wait until spring to plant summer-flowering bulbs. Some flowering plants are less hardy to cold and freeze than others. It is best to avoid planting those in fall, especially if you are on the low edge of their hardiness zone. If you live in a cold, damp area, you might want to wait until spring to transplant any flowering perennial subject to root rot, which can occur when roots sit in moist, cool soil.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7715. Accusing University Lecturer Who Called Police of "Blatant Racial Profiling" Leads to $37,500 Defamation Verdict

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

You can see the verdict form, from Thursday, here. The jury had asked whether they could suggest additional remedies besides the money:

But the court referred the jury to Instruction No. 10, which focused solely on monetary damages.

The backstory, from the opinion this April Judge Rebecca Pennell (E.D. Wash.) in Riera v. Central Wash. Univ., which let the case go forward:

Mr. Riera was employed in a fixed term, non-tenure track faculty at Central Washington University (CWU)…. On the morning of April 1, [2024,] Mr. Riera called the CWU police to report an older, "apparently homeless," woman wandering around Samuelson Hall. He said he wanted to make a report "before things get … out of control." An officer reported to Samuelson Hall and confirmed the identity of the woman as a CWU professor. No further action was taken by campus police or Mr. Riera.

The CWU professor shared her experience with two colleagues. The colleagues immediately filed bias complaints with CWU, alleging the target of Mr. Riera's call—a Black woman—had been the victim of racial profiling.

This led to a great deal of institutional response, including a discussion at a faculty senate meeting. Defendant Erdman, "a lecturer at CWU and member of the faculty senate, emailed unofficial minutes [of the meeting] to non-tenured faculty," and her notes included this:

Without naming names or describing the incident, [CWU President] Wohlpart expressed his outrage at a recent unconscionable incident on campus.

From my own knowledge, I think I can tell you the basics: It was an incident of blatant racial profiling. Campus police were called because a person of color was sitting quietly in the lobby of a CWU building for a brief interval. The person turned out to be a highly distinguished faculty member—but was compelled to produce and show ID before being left in peace.

(I must remark that this is outrageous on multiple levels. All CWU buildings are public; they belong to the State of Washington and its people. Anyone may sit in the lobby of any of our buildings. There was no reason at all to call the police—except, I guess, that this was a person of color.)

Wohlpart called the incident "unacceptable" and said that Central is working to see to it that such a thing doesn't happen again on our campus….

Riera sued Erdman, among others, and the court allowed his defamation claim to go forward in part:

[M]ost of [Erdman's] statements cannot be characterized as false. The only exception is Defendant Erdman's statement that what happened on April 1 "was an incident of blatant racial profiling." A jury could conclude this statement falsely asserts that the person who called police on April 1 engaged in intentional racial profiling. And, given widely-shared public records revealed Mr. Riera as the caller, a jury could also conclude Defendant Erdman's statement was about Mr. Riera.

Defendants argue that regardless of truth or falsity, Defendant Erdman's statement cannot be considered defamatory because it falls under the common interest privilege. "The common interest privilege applies with the declarant and the recipient have a common interest in the subject matter of the communication." The privilege applies to "persons involved in the same organization, partnerships, associations, or enterprises who are communicating on matters of common interest." Examples include officers of a nonprofit association or partners to a partnership. The privilege arises "when parties need to speak freely and openly about subjects of common organizational or pecuniary interest." …

If the privilege exists, it can be lost in two circumstances (1) if the speaker is not acting in the ordinary course of their work or (2) the speaker's statement was made with actual malice; i.e., reckless disregard for the truth. Whether the privilege has been lost under either scenario is a question of fact.

Here, the parties appear to agree that members of CWU's faculty senate are members of the same organization who share a common interest. The dispute lies in whether an exception applies.

The Court concludes there are issues of fact regarding whether Defendant Erdman's statements fell outside the scope of the privilege. Going to the first exception, Defendant Erdman had no official responsibility for taking notes at faculty meetings and she was not required to share her notes with other members of the senate faculty. A jury could therefore conclude that her statements were outside the ordinary course of her work as a member of a senate.

With respect to the second exception, Defendant Erdman was not a witness to the April 1 incident and no investigation had yet taken place. A jury could therefore conclude Defendant Erdman was reckless in asserting that the call to CWU police was an act of blatant racial profiling…. [T]he allegations against Defendant Erdman raise questions of fact that must be resolved by a jury.

Note that the court granted summary judgment as to plaintiff's defamation claim against President Wohlpart; as to plaintiff's defamation claim against CWU, the court stated that "Mr. Riera appears to have abandoned this claim and the summary judgment briefing does not describe how CWU as an institution may be liable for defamation." The one remaining defendant at trial was Erdman.

UPDATE 11/3/26 4:45 pm: I had originally written that the claims against the University were abandoned, but apparently plaintiff's counsel is disputing that, and intends to appeal the court's dismissal of the claims against CWU and Wohlpart. I've revised the post to say that the court stated the claim was abandoned.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7713. FBI Operation Summer Heat 2.0 Nets Thousands of Violent Crime Arrests

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

In four months, the violent crime initiative also seized enough fentanyl to kill 52 million people

The FBI and its law enforcement partners are announcing the results of Summer Heat 2.0, a four-month violent crime initiative that resulted in 8,927 arrests, the seizure of deadly fentanyl and cocaine, and 5,013 dangerous illegally possessed weapons taken off American streets.

“This year’s Summer Heat was our second straight nationwide offensive to crush violent crime all over the country, and the results were outstanding,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Even after last year’s unprecedented numbers, all 56 FBI field offices stepped up and delivered even higher numbers this year—arresting almost 9,000 subjects, up 3% from Summer Heat last year; seizing 63% more fentanyl; identifying or locating 1,410 children, 34% higher than last year; and recovering over 5,000 weapons, up 120% from 2025. Major cities across America saw increases as high as 80% in arrests compared to last summer alone. When this FBI elevated ‘crushing violent crime’ to one of our top priorities, we moved 2,000 FBI personnel out of Washington and permanently into the field—making the decisive call to go on offense. This FBI isn’t waiting for violent criminals, drug traffickers, and weapons dealers to devastate our communities any longer. As a result, under the Trump administration’s leadership, we have achieved the most prolific reduction in violent crime in U.S. history.”  Between June 1 and September 20, the FBI and its 56 field offices surged resources alongside state and local partners to execute federal warrants on violent criminals and fugitives, dismantle violent gangs and transnational criminal organizations, identify and rescue child victims, and resolve violent crime cases in Indian Country.

The FBI’s Summer Heat 2.0 initiative achieved additional victories with 687 kilograms of fentanyl seized: an amount equal to 52 million lethal doses. Of the 8,927 arrests, more than 5,900 arrests fell under the FBI’s violent crime and gang program.

A Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) takedown across two states, Operation Turf War, kicked off the FBI’s 2026 Summer Heat initiative. FBI Pittsburgh, in coordination with West Virginia’s HSTF, netted 32 narcotics and weapons-related arrests. In a separate effort in July 2026, FBI Los Angeles executed 17 federal arrest warrants and 49 search warrants in connection with Operation Hard Ball. The operation united FBI Los Angeles with law enforcement from Canada and Europe to investigate an organized crime group accused of a litany of criminal acts. And in yet another example of the success of Operation Summer Heat, FBI San Juan and its partners led Operation Taking Back West, which resulted in the indictment of 81 members of a violent criminal gang.   The FBI first launched the Summer Heat initiative for three months in 2025 to deploy a multi-pronged offensive to crush violent crime. The announcement of Operation Summer Heat 2.0 results follows on the heels of historic drops in crime across the U.S., according to the FBI’s 2025 UCR Summary of Reported Crimes in the Nation.

#7712. It’s OK to wear Milwaukee Brewers attire in court, judge says

A Wisconsin county judge is allowing people to wear Milwaukee Brewers attire in county courtrooms to celebrate the team’s recent World Series victory.

Following the Milwaukee Brewers’ historic World Series victory Wednesday, a Wisconsin county judge issued an order allowing people to wear Milwaukee Brewers attire in county courtrooms through the end of the official victory parade.

Waukesha County Presiding Judge Michael P. Maxwell, who consulted first with the chief judge and the clerk of court, issued the order after the Brewers captured their first-ever World Series title in franchise history, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday, Fox6 News Milwaukee reports.

“While every day our courts deal with very serious issues, like child custody disputes and holding criminals accountable, the last few weeks have seen Brewer fever in many off-the-record conversations between lawyers, parties and court staff,” Maxwell wrote in a statement.

“We thought that this could be one small way we could recognize this historic achievement by the Milwaukee Brewers organization and let folks in the court system participate in celebrating with all Wisconsin,” he added.

#7709. A Ken Paxton Moment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

As Texas AG, Paxton's done a lot of controversial and in-my-opinion unwise things, but this is the one that sticks in my craw

I have stayed away from discussing any of the many important electoral contests that will be (hopefully) decided today.  But given that he is at the center of one of the most hotly-contested Senate seats, I can't help being reminded of his conduct during the campaign to overturn the 2020 election results, and what may have been the lowest of many low points in Ken Paxton's career to date.

In December 2020, when he was Attorney General of Texas, Paxton was the attorney of record in a lawsuit against the states of Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, seeking to overturn the 2020 election results in those states.  He petitioned the Supreme Court to exercise its original jurisdiction to hear the case, and to do so on an expedited basis. [See my blog posting at the time here; Paxton's papers filed at SCOTUS are posted here].

Expert analysis using a commonly accepted statistical test raises serious questions as to the integrity of this election. The probability of former Vice President Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States—Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin—independently given President Trump's early lead in those States as of 3 a.m. on November 4, 2020, is less than one in a quadrillion, or 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000. For former Vice President Biden to win these four States collectively, the odds decrease to less than one in a quadrillion to the fourth power (i.e., 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000^4).

The same less than one in a quadrillion statistical improbability [applies to] Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States. . . . Again, the statistical improbability of Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in these four States collectively is 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000.

Put simply, there is substantial reason to doubt the voting results in the Defendant States.

Indeed there is!  Prima facie proof of fraud in the counting of ballots, I'd say. But only, of course, it it's correct, or at least close to correct. But it's not correct.  It is, as anyone with a knowledge of elementary statistics would have recognized immediately, simply and laughably wrong. The technical term is, I believe, "utter bullshit." I explain why here.  The probability that Joe Biden would end up with a majority in any of those is not one in a quadrillion - let alone one in a quadrillion to the 4th power (!), which is approximately equal to the probability that the sun will rise in the West tomorrow, and will have developed the capacity for human speech - nor anything close to one in a quadrillion.

Hey, we all make mistakes, right? What is most disgraceful about this episode is not that Paxton screwed up in his brief to the Court; it is that he never acknowledges his error, either publicly or, more importantly perhaps, to the Court. His assertion that the probability that Biden actually carried these States was equal to the probability that you would pick the single blue marble from a collection of 1,000,000,000,000,000 marbles, is a falsehood, and it is one that is at the core of his argument, in a case that was of grave importance to the future of the country. If Paxton didn't catch that falsehood before he filed his papers with the Court, he's merely a lousy lawyer, which I suppose is nothing to get too worked up about, given that there always will be plenty of lousy lawyers out there. But if he doesn't acknowledge that he has misled the Court after those misstatements are revealed - if he doesn't tell the Court that it has to ignore the part of his argument that relied on this incorrect understanding of statistics - then he's in a much more sinister category.

That this is the candidate whom the Texas Republican party chose as its candidate for U.S. Senate speaks volumes about the current state of the Rule of Law in this Administration. I'm sure that Mr. Paxton is looking forward, assuming the results go his way, to forging a close working relationship with Attorney General Todd Blanche, who is similarly scrupulous in his adherence to fundamental Rule of Law principles (as in the Slush Fund fraud-on-the-court perpetrated by Blanche and the DOJ].

David Post is currently an Adjunct Scholar at the Cato Institute, and was previously a professor at Beasley School of Law at Temple University.

#7707. Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

after noting that many of plaintiff's filings contained seeming AI hallucinations, despite assertions in plaintiff's filings that all the citations were valid.

From Judge Aileen Cannon (S.D. Fla.) in Paulk v. Larva Labs, LLC, decided in June but just posted on Westlaw:

This case presents a dispute over Defendant's alleged fraudulent interference with Plaintiff's Non-Fungible Tokens ("NFTs"). Plaintiff's Complaint, initially filed in Florida state court on January 20, 2026, alleges that in June 2017, Plaintiff used a publicly available software tool to generate 141 NFTs on the Ethereum blockchain. Each of these NFTs represents ownership of a unique CryptoPunk that was part of the first version of CryptoPunks ("V1"), a pioneering generative art project consisting of 24x24 pixel portraits. To create the NFTs, Plaintiff paid only nominal "gas fees" (i.e., fees paid to third parties who validate transactions on the Ethereum blockchain), and the NFTs "have remained in [a] dormant wallet" controlled to this day by Plaintiff.

Plaintiff alleges that, on June 23, 2017, Defendant "deployed" a second version of CryptoPunks ("V2"), "claiming V1 contained a 'bug.'" The Complaint then asserts that Defendant "suppressed V1 marketplace activity while promoting V2 as the sole authoritative collection, rendering Plaintiff's assets commercially impaired". Based on these allegations, the Complaint asserts causes of action for fraudulent concealment (Count I), unjust enrichment (Count II), declaratory relief (Count III), and injunctive relief (Count IV), seeking unspecified monetary damages and an injunction.

The court discussed various procedural issues, and then added:

As a separate matter, the Court is concerned more generally about the plethora of legal filings seemingly prepared by artificial intelligence and submitted by Plaintiff that make frivolous and unsupported arguments to the Court [see, e.g., ECF Nos. 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 26, 26-1, 31, 32, 33]. As an example, Plaintiff makes the obviously incorrect submission that the citizenship of Defendant's counsel can be considered in determining complete diversity.

And many of Plaintiff's filings contain disclaimers to the Court, expressly certifying "that every legal authority, statutory provision, rule of procedure, and historical case citation referenced within [the filings] has been independently read, analyzed, verified, and cross-referenced against official federal and state legal repositories." In each of these filings, "Plaintiff guarantees that every cited case stands as valid, binding law within the United States Supreme Court and the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals, possesses an active and unchecked standing, and accurately represents the procedural postures asserted." And he expressly warrants that he has not included any "fictitious or unverified citations," and that he has "manually double-checked" each case to ensure that it "support[s] Plaintiff's cause perfectly, ensuring that no unverified or 'hallucinated' data is presented to the Court."

No doubt Plaintiff's artificial intelligence legal counsel told him to say all this. And the AI certainly had the right idea—litigants should not make misrepresentations to the Court. Unfortunately, Plaintiff did not practice what his artificial counsel preached. Instead, he cites to "Snapper v. Redan, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)"—a case which does not exist—for the proposition that "when a company's chief legal representative has been sent formal notification at a publicly advertised professional office location, the entity cannot assert an administrative breakdown within its secondary commercial mail hubs as an equitable basis to vacate an otherwise valid default". Notwithstanding the made-up citation, the case Plaintiff means to cite, Snapper, Inc. v. Redan (11th Cir. 1999), is an Eleventh Circuit case that says nothing of the sort. Instead, Snapper established that federal appellate courts have jurisdiction to review remand orders based on the enforcement of contractual forum selection clauses. It does not mention vacatur, or default, or even mail—and it certainly does not stand for the extremely narrow proposition for which Plaintiff cites it.

In light of all this, Plaintiff has violated his duty of candor to the Court and has committed a Rule 11 violation…. [T]he Court [therefore] imposes filing sanctions as follows:

Plaintiff failed to respond to the motion to dismiss, and in a later opinion the court granted that motion.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Alexander Suvorov, 52, a Russian national, has been charged by a criminal complaint with three counts related to the unlawful exporting of micro-electronic components from the United States to Russia via a front company based in Hong Kong.

“Those, like the defendant, as alleged, who seek to enrich themselves by evading economic sanctions on Russia, must understand that their actions carry serious consequences and will not be tolerated,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney John A. Sarcone III for the Northern District of New York. “My office, working together with the FBI and the Department of Commerce, will continue to aggressively prosecute these types of cases and hold offenders accountable to the fullest extent of the law. This historic extradition shows that we will fly over 3,800 miles to locate and bring to justice those who threaten national security.”

“Alexander Suvorov was the alleged mastermind behind an international procurement network that illegally supplied buyers in Russia with American-made electronic components that have military applications,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “His extradition to face charges here in the U.S. demonstrates the FBI's commitment to keeping sensitive, export-controlled technology out of the hands of the Russian military. We will continue working with our law enforcement, intelligence, private sector, and international partners to bring to justice all who attempt to arm our adversaries at the expense of our citizens and our national security.”

“The Bureau of Industry and Security is committed to strong enforcement,” said Special Agent in Charge Jonathan Carson of the U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security New York Field Office. “Working closely with out law enforcement partners, we will continue to uncover and disrupt illicit procurement and diversion networks wherever they operate.”

Suvorov was extradited from Sweden to the Northern District of New York on Oct. 15 and is expected to have his initial appearance on Oct. 16 in Albany, New York.

The complaint filed against Suvorov alleges that between about March 2022 and April 2023, Suvorov led an illicit procurement network responsible for unlawfully exporting U.S. electronic components out of the United States to Russia. One of the procurement network’s main goals was to fraudulently obtain dual-use electronic components — that is, electronic components with both civilian and military applications — from U.S. companies for shipment to Russia. As alleged in the complaint, Suvorov’s primary role in the procurement network was to maintain front companies based in Hong Kong, including GS Group Limited, which the procurement network used to order electronic components from U.S. companies in an effort to conceal that the end users of the components were in Russia, and to then transship, via Hong Kong, the components from the U.S. companies to the end users in Russia. Suvorov and his companies are also alleged to have sent multiple wires to various U.S. companies to pay for the electronic components. Some of the components unlawfully purchased and exported to Russia by Suvorov and his procurement network can be used in military communication and radar systems, as well as precision location systems.

Count 1 of the complaint alleges conspiracy to commit international promotional money laundering and carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $500,000. Count 2 alleges conspiracy to commit outbound smuggling and carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $250,000. Count 3 alleges conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act (ECRA) and carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release, and a fine of $1,000,000. A federal district judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

The FBI and Department of Commerce are investigating the case. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs secured the extradition of Suvorov with the assistance of the Swedish Authorities.

Trial Attorney Garrett Coyle of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Rick Belliss for the Northern District of New York are prosecuting the case.

#7703. Choosin' Texas I Can Tell

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A few moments ago, the networks called the Texas Senate and Governor races for the Democratic candidates. Those outcomes will get a lot of attention. But of significant interest will be the downballot judicial races in Texas.

This year, four of the nine seats on the Texas Supreme Court were on the ballot. Unless something unexpected happens, all four will lose: Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock, Justice James P. Sullivan, Justice Kyle Hawkins, and Justice Brett Busby. These are all brilliant judges. Two of them clerked on the United States Supreme Court. Chief Justice Blacklock has been a strong leader, following in the footsteps of Chief Justice Nathan Hecht. But the qualifications do not matter. Everything was on the party line. The Texas Supreme Court will now have five Republican members and four Democratic members. One might expect a number of 5-4 cases for controversial cases. Then again, the Chief Justice is now the administrator of the state court system, which entails some important responsibilities.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (the court of last resort for criminal cases) had three seats on the ballot. Again, unless something happens, all three will lose. There will still be a six-member conservative majority. I don't see too much changing on that Court.

Recently, the Fifteenth Court of Appeals was created as a statewide constitutional court. Virtually all suits against the government are routed to that court. (Think of something like the D.C. Circuit.) All three members of that court were on the ballot. Unless something happens, all three will lose. The Court will now have 100% Democratic members. I would expect a lot mandamus suits to the Texas Supreme Court.

I haven't had time to go through the returns from the local courts, but it appears that most of the incumbent republican judges will lose office. This will be an even bigger bloodbath than 2018, when the Beto wave wiped out nearly all of the Republican judges in Houston, Austin, Dallas, and other large cities. So much judicial experience for non-controversial judges will go down the tube.

The Governor of Texas is fairly weak, as compared to other states, but he does have the power to appoint new members of the Texas Supreme Court and other courts when vacancies arise. Recently, the Texas legislature created a new Texas Business Court. This court was designed to compete with Delaware. Many of the current Texas business courts are not likely to be reappointed. This election will significantly affect businesses that chose to make Texas their headquarters. Speaking of which…

The Texas Attorney General Race will also likely go to the Democratic candidate. I would suspect that all of the conservative strategic litigation cases brought by Attorney General Paxton will be dismissed. Indeed, it is conceivable that the new Texas Attorney General would not defend the Texas Ten Commandments Law if cert is granted. (The BIO will be filed soon.) The Texas Attorney General will also not bring original jurisdiction actions before the Supreme Court of Texas. Going forward, all of the strategic forums in Texas will be severely underutilized. The only court where the Texas Attorney General might file cases will be in Austin. I should note that one seat on the Western District of Texas remained vacant for two years, and will likely remain vacant. But beyond the strategic litigation, the Texas Attorney General will now be able to investigate all of the corporations that moved to Texas. There are a lot of them.

What about judicial nominees? Despite my best efforts, Judge Southwick will get the last laugh. Todd Butler will almost certainly be confirmed. But the Fifth Circuit will likely be a lot quieter, given the lack of Texas Attorney General cases. I also hope this means that Judge Rudofsky will get a vote, as that Eighth Circuit seat would remain vacant for the foreseeable future. Indeed, the Eighth Circuit may be the only viable forum for a Republican AG to bring cases starting in 2028.

Going forward, Senators Cruz and Talarico will have to agree on blue slips for District Court nominees. Still, I suspect zero nominees will get a vote over the next two years unless there is some deal struck with the Senate Democrats.

What about Justices Alito and Thomas? They did what Justice Breyer could not--resist the pressure. I hope they live long and prosper.

Ultimately, I'm reminded of something I tell my students--we are never more than two years away from a midterm election. Despite threats about fascism and totalitarianism, the people are able to effect change.

NEXT: Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7697. Lawyer, business partner accused of defrauding cannabis investor of $750K

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows. (Image from Shutterstock)

A Los Angeles attorney and his business partner are accused of paying for their personal expenses with investor money instead of funding business-to-consumer cannabis trade shows, including the unsuccessful Green Street Festival in 2022.

A Los Angeles County court complaint filed by investor Jamie Chisick alleged that attorney Joshua Shelton of the Winston Wolfe Law Firm and his business partner, Rama Mayo, took $750,000 for a 15% ownership stake in the Green Street Symposium.

According to the Oct. 19 complaint, Shelton and Mayo, cannabis entrepreneurs, promised to organize large trade events that would attract thousands of attendees and generate “millions of dollars in revenue,” according to coverage on Law360.

Chisick obtained documents that he said shows that his money had been used for “personal payments, including but not limited to private jets, health insurance, bar dues (Shelton) and general overhead unrelated to GSS operations.”

The 2022 Green Street Festival brought in about $190,000 with about $178,000 refunded. A 2023 festival with projections of attracting over 10,000 attendees and up to $4.7 million in revenue drew a smaller crowd and did not produce a profit.

Chisick seeks to recover his investment and punitive damages, according to the complaint.

#7696. Crime in Texas, Trial in Texas, Confession to Clergy in North Carolina: Which Law Applies?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

By design, our American legal system largely lets different states make different rules. Most states recognize a tort of disclosure of private facts; some don't. A few recognize a tort of alienation of affections; most don't. Some states allow first-cousin marriage; others don't. Some set a one-year statute of limitations for defamation; some set it at two or three years. The list goes on.

Much conduct happens in one state, and the resulting disputes arise in the courts of that state. But other matters are multi-state affairs. Indeed, some are multinational affairs, even though they end up in one country's courts: What happens if a contract was entered into in France, performed in Canada, but plaintiff sues defendant over an alleged breach where they now both live, in Illinois?

There is therefore a body of law called "conflict of laws" (or "choice of laws") that tries to resolve these questions. As it happens, that is itself state law, so different states can have different conflicts rules, with at least three major schools of thought on the matter. (Think that's confusing? Don't get me started on renvoi and dépeçage.)

Here's a scenario that arose in the recent Texas Campbell v. State case:

Appellant was charged, in Harris County, Texas, with murdering his girlfriend. His girlfriend was killed in Texas. And then Appellant went to his mother's home in North Carolina.

While he was in North Carolina, Appellant's mother urged Appellant to speak with a bishop on the telephone. While he was on the phone with the bishop, and allegedly with his mother still in the room, Appellant made a statement admitting that he killed his girlfriend. During trial, the bishop was called to testify as a witness about the contents of Appellant's statement….

Texas Rule of Evidence 505(b) sets forth a clergy-penitent testimonial privilege:

A communicant has a privilege to refuse to disclose and to prevent any other person from disclosing a confidential communication by the communicant to a clergy member in the clergy member's professional capacity as a spiritual advisor.

{[A communication is] "confidential" if made privately and not intended for further disclosure except to other persons present to further the purpose of the communication.}

But though all states have some clergy-penitent privilege, North Carolina courts have interpreted the N.C. privilege statute as not applying "when the disclosures are made in the presence of a third party," apparently with no exception (as in Texas and some other states) for people "present to further the purpose of the communication."

Gonzalez v. State (2001), a precedent from the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (Texas's highest court for criminal laws) relied on the Restatement (Second) of Conflict of Laws and its "most significant relationship test" when determining which state's law applies. (The Restatement is an influential work compiled by the American Law Institute, a generally highly respected organization of lawyers, judges, and academics; many courts find it persuasive, as the Texas court did in Gnozalez.)

And the court concluded, citing the comments to the Restatement, "that the state where the communication took place is generally the state with the most significant relationship." Based on that precedent, a Texas appellate court in Campbell held that North Carolina law applied, and that the communication was admissible.

But Texas Court of Criminal Appeals Judge Kevin Yeary took a different view dissenting from denial of review in September:

[T]he Restatement is not the law of this state. When our Texas Rules of Evidence were adopted, this state did not incorporate language from the Restatement demanding that a different rule should apply when a clergy-communicant statement is made outside of our state's borders.

There is also no textual basis for any argument that any conflict between the laws of another state and our state's Rules of Evidence should be considered. Our state's rule on clergy-communications contains no exception for circumstances in which such a communication occurs in a different state. There appears to be no true legal reason to even dwell on such a question, unless perhaps a court just does not like our rule of evidence!

We are not bound by the Restatements of the Laws. We should not consider ourselves to be controlled by them in any regard. We should also not consider ourselves, or our lower courts, to be at liberty to simply adopt any Restatement as the law of this state, even if we think it has expressed a good idea.

Judges are not elected to play the role of policy makers. If anyone in this state thinks we should change a rule or a policy expressed in a rule, then that person should raise the matter as a proposed change to our Texas Rules of Evidence. In that way, the matter could be considered by a rules committee, and the committee could then consider public input before deciding whether to amend our rule.

We have rules of evidence that are written down, with pesky little things called words—that mean things. Presumably, the people who adopted our Texas Rules of Evidence fully considered them, and the words in them, before adopting them. We should consider whether the words in our actual rules are enough….

On its own terms, the rule is quite clear. It does not contemplate the situation in which the statement is made to clergy when the communicant is out of state. When our courts, and when we, pretend that our rule of evidence demands a different set of rules for when a communication occurs in another state, we destroy our own credibility as an equal arbiter of the law. Our courts should simply follow the language of our own Rules. And we should lead the lower courts in that direction by granting review in this case to show them the way….

Under Texas Rule of Evidence Rule 505(a)(3), Appellant's mother's presence might not serve to preclude Appellant from asserting the clergy-communicant privilege. It is therefore conceivable that, if the Texas Rule had been applied, Appellant might have been able to prevent the bishop from testifying.

The Restatement (Second) of Conflicts of Law § 139 (1) states: "(1) Evidence that is not privileged under the local law of the state which has the most significant relationship with the communication will be admitted, even though it would be privileged under the local law of the forum, unless the admission of such evidence would be contrary to the strong public policy of the forum." It is seems to me that there exist strong arguments that allowing the admission of the communication at issue in this case is against the strong public policy of Texas. By its own terms, Texas's clergy-communicant privilege can even apply when made in the presence of a third person; and Texas rule makers certainly added this section intentionally. Tex. R. Evid. 505(a)(3) ("A communication is 'confidential' if made privately and not intended for further disclosure except to other persons present to further the purpose of the communication.") We should look for the "strong public policy" of the state in the plain text of the rule.

I should note that the subject of conflicts of law is largely about deciding when a foreign law should be used even when a local statute would on its face appear to apply. The theory is that legislatures generally write statutes with an eye towards local matters, and can't be expected to consider all the complications that arise in the rare multi-state cases; better leave that to courts to figure out using judge-made choice-of-law rules, the theory goes. But Judge Yeary argues that courts ought to take a more textualist approach to such questions.

I'm inclined towards the choice-of-law rule applied in Gonzalez, under which courts should apply the law of the place where the communication happened. (Of course, that can still leave a question of what happens if the communication is by Zoom, and the clergy member is in one state and the congregant is in another.) But in any event, I thought this was an interesting question to pass along.

NEXT: Today in Supreme Court History: November 4, 1992

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.
